# Hardware Collision Kill Switch for Strain Wave Mounts: Prior Art and Requirements

## Question

Strain wave (harmonic drive) mounts have enough torque that a camera or OTA
striking a tripod or pier can be damaged. The proposal is a normally-closed
switch mounted on the protected device. If it is pressed, DC power to the
mount is cut, and it stays cut until someone intervenes by hand. It is meant
to be independent of all software and to work on any mount that holds
position when unpowered.

This document asks:

1. Does such a device exist, or has it been discussed?
2. Does the premise hold — do strain wave mounts stay put when power is cut?
3. What protection do mounts already ship?
4. What requirements can be borrowed from adjacent fields?

Supporting detail is in the four reference files:
[prior art](references/prior-art.md),
[power-loss behavior](references/power-loss-behavior.md),
[built-in protection](references/built-in-protection.md),
[E-stop requirements](references/estop-requirements.md).
Sources are in [citations](citations.md).

## Methodology

- Search used `multi_search.py`. Only one engine wave answered (candidate
  set duckduckgo, yahoo, google); the other wave (mojeek, brave,
  startpage) failed on every query. 68 web queries and 2 scholarly
  (OpenAlex/Crossref) queries ran; 6 web queries returned nothing.
- Pages were fetched through the sandbox fetch service. Cloudy Nights and
  Stargazers Lounge returned Cloudflare challenges; those pages were read
  through the r.jina.ai reader. ZWO forum threads were read through the
  forum's JSON API. On 2026-10-06 the operator supplied 9 pages the service
  could not read as browser-printed PDFs ([85]–[92]; one was scanned and
  read by OCR). One schematic image was fetched directly [93]. Every such
  citation is marked in [citations](citations.md).
- Four dimension analyses and one gap-fill pass extracted quotes from the
  fetched text. Two citation auditors (splitting the citations between
  them), one consistency reviewer and a re-verification pass checked the
  output (see [audit/](audit/)).

## Findings

### 1. Prior art: no exact match found; the principle is discussed

No product, patent, or reported working build of a **camera-mounted contact
switch that cuts mount power and latches until manual reset** appeared in
the fetched sources ([prior art](references/prior-art.md)). Close relatives
do exist:

- **Professional radio telescopes.** One poster recalls micro-switch "hard
  limit switches" struck by "pushers" that "tripped the drive controller at
  the HW-level". Recovery: "it needed to be manually driven out of limits by
  someone at the telescope" [2]. This is the nearest match to the proposal,
  but it is one person's hedged recollection.
- **Amateur relay builds, triggered by position or communication loss
  rather than contact.**
  - An Arduino and accelerometer relay cuts AP1200 power outside an RA
    angle; "Manual recovery is necessary" [3].
  - ADG MountWatcher's watchdog relay cuts mount power if PC communication
    is lost [4].
  - A shelved accelerometer build "kills the power to the mount" in a no-go
    zone [1].
  - After a Wave 150i crash [6], its owner built a reed switch and relay
    limit (September 2025; "Just tested it and it works well"). With it the
    mount "cannot go more than about 10 degrees passed horizontal", and he
    says: "At least now this is not possible as the mount gets turned off"
    [85]. The power path and the reset are not described; he says he posted
    a wiring diagram, which was not reached.
- **Contact-triggered power cuts, suggested but not built.**
  - In the same thread, a poster proposes a micro switch "on the pier
    through which I would run the 12V to the mount. That would break the
    power to the mount when the scope gets close and touches the lever"
    [85]. This is the nearest suggestion to the proposal, with the switch on
    the pier instead of the payload.
  - In 2016 a remote imager recommended "hardware safety switches" that
    "kill power to your mount via a simple relay". He wrote "I use power
    poles and just have a NO (normally open) switch", and a later post
    corrects this to normally-closed switches in the power cord that "cut
    power to your mount if it hits" [86]. Whether the switch was installed,
    and whether it is position- or contact-triggered, is unclear.
  - In 2017 someone suggested a "whisker-style limit switch" wired as an NC
    E-stop in line with mount power [5].
- **Explicit endorsement of the principle.** A December 2025 Cloudy Nights
  thread contains an explicit argument for "a contactor to break the power
  to motor" driven by collision sensors, from a poster citing professional
  safety-system experience [1]. The same thread calls software hard stops "a
  total violation of the fail-safe concept" [2], and asks the open question
  "Does it power off the mount, or just stop? Recovery methods would also be
  necessary." [1]
- **The posted circuit is not fail-safe (inference).** That poster's
  attached schematic [93] uses normally-open reed switches that energize a
  relay to cut the drive motor. A broken wire therefore disables the
  protection, and nothing latches: power returns once the magnet moves
  away. The proposal here differs on both points.

The pattern: the community has discussed hardware power cutting since at
least 2016 [86], and builds it for **position** limits and **communication
loss**. A **contact** trigger with a **latched manual reset** is suggested
but not reported as built. No source puts a *contact switch* on the payload
(sensors on the moving part are proposed [1]); the closest contact-switch
suggestion puts it on the pier [85]. This rests on a single-wave search, so treat it as "not found", not
"does not exist".

### 2. The premise — "on power loss the mount stays where it was" — is only partly true

This is the most important finding for the design
([power-loss behavior](references/power-loss-behavior.md)).

- **Most documented strain wave brakes are RA only.**
  - ZWO AM5: "Power-oﬀ Brake RA Axis Only" [29]. ZWO staff: "Only the RA
    axis has a brake." [21]
  - ZWO AM3: RA only [31].
  - Pegasus NYX-101: RA only [36].
  - MLAstro SAL-33: RA only, per a third-party guide [39].
  - iOptron HAE: brakes on both RA and DEC [34]. iOptron's HEM27 and HAEc
    manuals do not name the axis [32], [35].
  - The Rainbow RST-135 manual mentions no brake [37]. A user says it has
    none on either axis [21].
- **Unbraked axes can move.**
  - The NYX-101 manual: unpowered "telescope weight can gradually start
    rotating the motor shaft, leading to a speed-up slewing of axes towards
    the ground" [36].
  - An AM5 owner saw DEC rotate after switch-off [21].
  - An AM5 teardown reports the RA brake is "a spring loaded solenoid
    brake" acting on the stepper, and lists "Belt failure" as a case where
    the load could freewheel [88]. It also reports a brake-removed test with
    14 lb in the worst RA position: "the load didnʼt fall", but once pushed
    "it kept going for a few seconds" and with "enough weight it will keep
    going till it hits the tripod/pier extension" [88]. This is the only
    empirical data point found, from one unit and one load. The same author
    says a balanced, unbraked DEC is "unlikely to move on it's own" [88].
  - Rainbow warns: "do not turn off the power while the right ascension
    axis is rotating... The right ascension axis rotates in the direction of
    gravity" [37].
- **Engineering sources conflict on back-drivability.**
  - A 1995 abstract: high-ratio units are "non-backdrivable" [54].
  - A gear maker: strain wave gears are "fundamentally reversible" and
    "complete self-locking cannot be guaranteed" [55].
  - A 2020 review gives finite back-driving starting torques [56].
  - Users who say the AM5 "should never drop" are offering opinion [40]; so
    is a user on the other side, who says "under enough load a strain wave can be back
    driven" [89].
  - A sponsored design primer hosted by Harmonic Drive LLC says strain wave gears "can withstand
    shock loads of up to five times the rated torque" but does not address
    back-driving [90].
- **A hard cut mid-slew is disputed.**
  - iOptron ("safely stop") and Pegasus ("instant safe stop") describe their brakes as stopping safely on
    unplanned power loss [34], [36].
  - Rainbow says not to cut power during RA rotation [37].
  - An industrial note says holding brakes used as stopping brakes are
    "potentially damaging", acceptable only for "infrequent use" [58].
  - A strain wave vendor lists "a hard stop from full speed" as a ratcheting
    cause [63].

**Implication (inference).** On AM5-class mounts, the kill switch converts
"motor pushing payload into tripod" into "RA braked, DEC free to back-drive
under imbalance". How far DEC moves depends on balance and on the gear's
back-driving torque, and no source measures it. Users suggest testing it
indoors [40]. The size of this risk is unknown.

### 3. The alternative ("resistance detection") exists but is partial

([built-in protection](references/built-in-protection.md))

- **ZWO AM5.** ZWO staff confirm stall detection exists but "will enable
  when the speed is R9(1440x)... it will not detect is in slow speed", with
  none at sidereal tracking [22]. The overnight crashes reported for the AM5
  happened while tracking [13], [22].
- **Rainbow RST-135.** The manual says it monitors "motor load, encoder
  error... to cut off the power and warn" [37].
- **Paramount (a worm-drive comparison).** "current limited... running
  into a fixed object will automatically stop slewing and tracking" [42].
- **The rest rely on position limits.** Software and firmware limits fail
  through PC reboots, clock and DST errors, manual moves, wrong zero
  positions, and collisions inside the allowed window [6], [12], [15],
  [18], [26], [46], [47], [53].

This partly supports the user's premise that the alternatives are
incomplete. For ZWO, iOptron, Pegasus and Sky-Watcher strain wave mounts, no
fetched document describes protection against a collision at tracking speed
that does not depend on position knowledge. The Rainbow RST-135 is the
exception: its manual documents load monitoring with a power cut [37]. It
gives no threshold, though, and does not say whether the monitoring is
active at tracking speed.

### 4. Requirements from adjacent fields

([E-stop requirements](references/estop-requirements.md); that file
numbers its items E1–E12)

**Scope caveat.** ISO 13850 defines an emergency stop as a function
"initiated by a single human action" [68]. A contact-tripped switch is
therefore not an E-stop under that standard. The clauses below are borrowed
by analogy for latching and reset behavior.

| # | Requirement | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | Latch on trip; stay off until reset by hand | ISO 13850 §4.1.1.2 [68] |
| R2 | No command (PC, app, hand controller) can move the mount while tripped | [68]; hand controllers bypass software interlocks [10] |
| R3 | Reset must not restart motion | [68], [71], [72] |
| R4 | Reset at the device, deliberately, after the obstacle is cleared | [70] |
| R5 | Release, reset and restart are separate steps | [73] |
| R6 | The stop must not create a new hazard (e.g. an unbraked axis falling) | [68] §4.1.1.5 |
| R7 | Do not defeat other safety functions such as brakes | [68] §4.1.1.4 |
| R8 | Complement to limits, not a substitute | [68] §4.1.1.3 |
| R9 | NC fail-safe wiring; positive-opening contacts that break welds | [76], [77], [80] |
| R10 | Interrupt power downstream of all controllers | [8] |
| R11 | Switch overtravel must absorb the mount's coast after cutoff | ISO 13856-2 terms [78]; inference |

Mount-specific requirements that follow from Findings 2 and 3 (inference):

| # | Requirement | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| R12 | Characterise unbraked-axis behavior (DEC on AM5/AM3/NYX/SAL-33) before relying on a power cut | [21], [29], [36], [39] |
| R13 | On re-enable, confirm the mount does not auto-resume tracking. Some mounts can ("may begin tracking when next powered up") | [44] |
| R14 | Plan for re-homing after the cut. AM5/AM5N lack absolute encoders, per a forum report. iOptron (HAE) and Pegasus store position. | [34], [36], [40] |
| R15 | Rate the switch at least to the mount supply, e.g. ZWO's recommended "12V 3A power for AM5 itself" (a supply recommendation, not a measured peak current) | [27] |

### 5. Counter-perspectives

1. **Contact-triggered means late.** "the collision already happened" [11].
   Overload ratcheting can occur "in a millisecond" [63]. A flexspline under
   load with a stationary input can buckle [64]. A switch limits how long
   the force lasts; it does not prevent the first impact.
2. **Coast after cutoff.** Once a strain wave axis is moving, the motor
   armature "acts like a flywheel, through a 100:1 reduction" [21]. Stopping
   distance after the cut is unmeasured.
3. **Cutting power breaks the software session** [9]. The intent is to
   stop the night, so this may be acceptable, but recovery is manual.
4. **False trips and placement.** Legitimate meridian flips can pass within
   about 5 mm of the tripod [1]. Switch placement has to change with each
   scope/camera configuration [86]. Sensors can misread (a roll-off-roof thread, applied by
   analogy) [11].
5. **Industry auto-resets and uses controllers.** Robot collision sensors
   signal a controller and reset automatically [81], [82]. The latched,
   controller-free design is a deliberate departure from that.
6. **Clutches and torque limiters solve a different part of the problem.**
   A slip clutch limits torque mechanically [67], and older mounts' RA
   clutches slip first [2]. Users say strain wave mounts lack clutches [7],
   [19]. Another poster's rhetorical premise is that some makers fit them,
   without naming any [41]. An industrial vendor says many harmonic drives
   carry brakes or clutches against crashes [57]. None of the strain wave
   mount manuals fetched ([29]–[39]) mentions a clutch.

## Limitations

- **Single-wave search.** Every web query was answered by one engine wave
  (candidate set duckduckgo, yahoo, google); ddgs does not report which
  engine answered. Coverage is one sample per query.
- **Reader-proxy content.** 28 citations, mostly Cloudy Nights and
  Stargazers Lounge, were read through r.jina.ai because the direct fetch
  hit Cloudflare. The audit compared against the reader rendering, not the
  original HTML.
- **Operator-supplied content.** 8 citations ([85]–[92]) come from PDFs the
  operator printed from pages the fetch service could not read (2026-10-06).
  [91] is an OCR transcription of a scanned ZWO manual (20 of 26 pages); it
  is used for paraphrase only. [92] turned out to be off-topic (dome homing).
  [93] is a schematic image; its topology is a transcription, not source
  text.
- **Unreached sources.**
  - Clarkey's wiring diagram in the SGL DIY section (his power path and
    reset).
  - CN 959669, and pages 2–4 of the AM5 teardown thread.
  - The RST-135 supplementary manual (login wall).
  - Full ISO/IEC standard texts. Only previews and vendor explainers were
    read.
- **Forum evidence is anecdotal.** No crash frequency can be derived.
- **No patent database search.** Only web-indexed patents were seen.
- **Recency.** Mount firmware changes quickly. ZWO staff statements date
  from 2023 [22], [26]; later firmware may differ.
